utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please be seated. Registrar, have the accused brought in, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First of all, I would like to be sure that the interpreters can hear me. Good afternoon to the interpreters, to the court reporters, to be sure that we're not having any technical problems. Good afternoon to both Defence and Prosecution counsel and to the accused. We will now continue with our testimony, and I give the floor either to Mr. Hayman or to Mr. Nobilo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President and Your Honours. I call General Tihomir Blaskic to testify, and I suggest that we proceed immediately with his examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. We're going to ask the accused to become a witness and that he take his place at the witness stand so that his testimony can begin, and we will start with the examination-in-chief. Please remain standing. Give the General his headset. Do you hear me? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours, I can hear you very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please remain standing for a few moments. Tell the Judges and the Court your name, your first name, your rank in the army, your last residence at the point when, of your own volition, you came to The Hague, and then you'll take an oath according to the Rules of Procedure and Evidence in force at this Tribunal. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I am General Tihomir Blaskic. My last residence was Zagreb, and I decided voluntarily to surrender from Zagreb to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Please tell us your place and date of birth.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I was born on 2nd November, 1960 in Kiseljak, municipality of Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Please be seated. Actually, take the oath first and then you'll be seated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Very well. You may now be seated for a rather long amount of time, according to your Defence counsel. Let me remind you that you have been indicted at the International Tribunal for three charges covered in our Statute, that is, Article 2, grave breach, Article 3, violations of the laws or customs of war, and Article 5, crime against humanity. In addition to our Rules of Procedure and Evidence, Rule 85 states that if he so desires, the accused may appear as a witness in his own defence. The Tribunal will not judge as to the appropriateness of this method of defence, which is the strategy which your Defence counsel have set into place, and having said this, you move from the accused, for the time you will testify, to a witness, like another witness, subject to the same obligations as another witness, including everything that has to do with truth of the testimony. Now, I think that we can begin. The Judges have agreed to the request of your counsel that the guards be at an appropriate distance so that you can be comfortable. Let me remind you that you must not speak too quickly; otherwise, the interpreters have difficulty following you. If necessary, you can use notes, but you cannot make statements. Perhaps you can do that at another time, but not general statements, but simply consult notes in order to refresh your memory. Relax, you are a witness like any other witness at this point, and you will now either begin with your free testimony or giving answers to the questions asked by your Defence counsel. As you know, you will then be cross-examined by the Prosecution. Mr. Nobilo, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Since you mentioned the notes, I would like to start off with a preliminary question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General Blaskic, could you describe to us or clarify to the Trial Chamber, in what way did you prepare for today's testimony? What did you contemplate using? What documents?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, at the time when I learned about the indictment which was issued against me, which was in November of 1995, I started preparing certain notes. Those were personal notes on the basis of the documents to which I had access. At the time, these were the war logbooks and certain orders which I had access to, and I noted down the dates and certain events with a special emphasis to the participants of those events. After having drafted these notes, I arrived here sometime in April of 1996 expecting that my trial would start on the 2nd of June, 1996. So in June of that year, I started giving a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor; however, the position of my Defence was that we should stop with that, and so I started working on my own statement based on the notes, and what I have in front of me is not my own statement. These are just dates and certain notes which I have here to refresh my memory regarding certain events in these two or three years of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. So the first area which I would like to ask you about, I would like you to give the Trial Chamber a brief account of your training and your career up until the point when you decided to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I will attempt to give you the information about my career, and I have to say that I regret that the best that I could come up with is not enough. As I said, I was born on the 2nd of November, 1960 in Kiseljak. This is in Kiseljak municipality. I come from a working-class family. My father was a miner and, later on, a driver. I also have a sister called Zrinka, she was born in 1966, and brother Mario who was born in 1972. He is disabled, and he still requires care. I lived in the local commune of Brestovsko, which is a local commune within the Kiseljak municipality. My neighbours were Bosnian Muslims. There were some Gypsies, there was one hamlet, and there were also Serbs. In this local commune, I completed my elementary schooling, and I lived there until I was 15, until 1975. After I completed elementary school, I continued my schooling in Zagreb, and I spent two years in Zagreb in school, and I specialised in chemical and technological studies. It was a civilian school. For my family, my schooling in Zagreb was a great financial burden because just the boarding costs were 115.000 dinars at that time, and my father's salary at that time was 130.000 dinars a month. So this financial situation and other reasons caused me to continue my school in the military high school called Fraternity and Unity in Belgrade. This is where I completed the third and fourth years of my high school in the years of 1966 and 1967.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, let me interrupt you for a moment. You said that the military academy or high school was called Fraternity and Unity. Can you explain to the Judges, who are not familiar with the local culture, what this name meant in the JNA doctrine and in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The former Yugoslavia was a multi-ethnic community. There were over 25 ethnic groups who lived in this territory, and this name, "Fraternity and Unity," meant some kind of equality in every respect, including participation of different ethnic groups and full respect of freedoms of every ethnic group to live its own culture, its own religion. For the JNA, it was considered as a foundation of the JNA set-up, and it was the basis of its morale and everything else that makes up an army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Go on now.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: After I completed this military high school, I was looking to apply to one of the military academies, and I decided to go to the military academy in Belgrade, which was for the army, and I chose to specialise in infantry. So I spent the first three years in Belgrade and the fourth year in Sarajevo, and on the 30th of July, 1983, I graduated at a common ceremony in Belgrade. Our training was structured as an eight-semester training. For the first two years, these were mostly general courses without specialising in any particular military disciplines, and in the third and fourth year, we had specialised courses for the most part. For one semester in the first year, we also had a military law course. Throughout my training at the military academy and my separation from my family between 1975 and 1983, I spent time in a boarding school, that is, I was in student homes and dormitories where I usually shared it with a Croat, a Slovenian, a Macedonian, an Albanian, and a member of another ethnic group, depending on whether the rooms were with two beds or four beds. After I completed school, between '83 and '87, I lived in the military hotels for singles, and we, again, had the same sleeping arrangements. There would be two or three beds per room. There would be a Croat, a Slovenian or a Muslim, and a Serb there. Throughout the schooling, we had internships where we were placed in different roles. At one point, I was in Ohrid in 1983 as just a simple conscript, and I spent two months there undergoing basic infantry training as a regular soldier. The next type of practical course was in 1982, I believe this could have been in April, in Belgrade, in the then Socialist Republic of Serbia. There, I was a commanding officer of a squad. The final practical course was in Niksic which was in the former Socialist Republic of Montenegro in April of 1983 where I had the duty of a commander of a platoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you that you carried out practical courses in three different republics of Yugoslavia, and you were a Croat from the fourth out of six former republics?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that in your room, in your dorm room, you would always have members of different ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Were these practical courses and this regiment, were members of different ethnic groups always mixed together, or was this something that was accidental or was that something that was part of the doctrine?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That was not accidental at all, especially not in the military high school and then the military academy. I also have additional experience of having lived in military hotels for single people the following four years. So that was definitely part of the JNA doctrine because they wanted to implement this equality, equal participation of different ethnic groups. A similar criteria also existed in the JNA units where, in commissions which were in charge of accommodation of new recruits, this was also taken into account, so that all ethnic groups who lived in the territory of the former Yugoslavia would participate.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did this approach contribute to a particular sense within the JNA?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Of course. Some of my colleagues were admitted at the age of 14, 15, at a time when they were still in their formative years, and this was a way for different ethnic groups to meet each other, and in the context of the army, this contributed to better understanding and to reaffirming of these basic principles of equality and rights, but also obligations, for everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: After you completed your training and after you graduated, what was your first job?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was assigned to service in the 9th Army Corps of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia which covered the area of the former Socialist Republic of Slovenia. My first post was the garrison in Ljubljana and later Pivka and then Postojna. In Ljubljana, I became commander of the cadets in the school of reserve officers, which was the size of a company, and it trained officers for the Territorial Defence units in Slovenia. After a period of time, the former JNA was reorganised, and in 1985, this unit was dissolved; in other words, it was reformed, and then I assumed the post of the assistant of the political science school in Ljubljana teaching the All People's Defence, and I was in this post until March of 1986. I was an assistant for certain courses there, it was for tactical topics, and I worked with Anton Tovornik, who was a major, and the fact that I spent a certain amount of time in the command of the 9th Army provided me access to some of the high-ranking officers in the 9th Army; and in conversations with them, I learned that I was designated to be transferred to the new garrison in Postojna. Around 28 December, 1985, I was invited by the chief of personnel from my former unit, this was the 14th regiment in Ljubljana, and he told me that I was designated to be transferred to the Postojna garrison where special forces were being established, they were known as "ready forces," and one of these units was supposed to be sent down to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me -- I believe at that time this region was called the Autonomous Province of Kosovo within the Socialist Republic of Serbia. What was going on down there? Why were these ready forces supposed to go down there and what would be their task down there?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Its exact name was the Socialist Autonomous Province of Kosovo, and this was a periodic practice by the JNA up until the time when the Pristina corps was formed. As early as 1979, and maybe even earlier, certain military units were sent to the Kosovo territory, and these units were primarily used to carry out predominantly police type of tasks. It was to be a demonstration of force for the purposes of intimidation of the local population, and I had some information about this from the chief of staff of the 14th proletarian regiment, Mr. Djilas, who, for a while, was deployed there with his unit. He had been transferred there from Bovec.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What type of information did you get? Why was this intimidation needed? What was the ethnic background of the population there? Can you shed more light on the events in Kosovo at that time?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: For the most part, the population was Muslim. They had identified themselves as Albanians. They were not happy with the arrangements and the rights which they had as a minority, they were demanding more freedoms, and at that time, their political representatives were expressing their disagreement with the policy which was dominant in the Socialist Republic of Serbia. The role of the unit was a demonstration of force in a way and probably the use of force depending upon the developing situations, because I know that occasionally it was used, and it was also to instil fear among the population in a sense that they would be much more cautious and that they would be aware of what could happen should such events escalate, that is, demonstrations and other activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In this type of security atmosphere which you described to us, which I think is linked to what is going on there today, what was your reaction? Did you accept that assignment or not?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I immediately, in this first conversation with the chief of service, the chief of personnel in the 14th regiment, I said immediately that I did not want to accept this post, and I publicly let him know that I did not want to be a part of this force which was to be sent to Kosovo, regardless of the consequences I might suffer. At that time, he said that this would be an act of disobedience, insubordination, and that I could be sanctioned for it. Following this conversation, I was again called in by his deputy, and the conversation was almost the same. I later talked to the assistant for morale in the 14th regiment, and my departure, that is, my discussion about my leaving for that assignment went on all the way until March of 1986. In the meantime, I had an official conversation with the commander of the battalion, with the deputy commander of the regiment itself, Major Uzelac. I made it very clear to everyone that I, under no circumstances, wanted to take on this assignment and take part in the units that would go to Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you explain to the Trial Chamber, how was the tour of duty in Kosovo treated in terms of compensation?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can tell you that the increase in Sarajevo was automatic. I know that units that were deployed in Kosovo in the '80s had a wartime supplement, that is, a supplement in salary which people would receive in case of war. There were additional benefits, such as additional vacation time, then advancement in career, accelerated promotion, and in some ways also priorities in getting apartments and preferred postings. Despite all these benefits, I could not accept assuming such a duty and taking such a post.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell the Court, please, whether you did go or whether you were able to side-step this assignment and what your career was like after that?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, I did not go on that assignment. I was transferred on the 6th of March, 1986, to the Pivka garrison, and I remember my first contacts very well. In that garrison, on the morning when I reported for duty for the first time, I met the chief of staff in the garrison, the Pivka garrison, he was Lieutenant Colonel Reljanovic, and he asked me on that morning, and I quote verbatim: "What have you done wrong to be sent to us here?" End of quotation. I reported to the commander, and I took over my duties. I was commander of the 2nd company in the 1st Battalion. What I noticed at that time --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Excuse me for interrupting you. What rank did you have at that point? Were you a captain? Were you a lieutenant? Perhaps I didn't listen carefully enough. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, at that time I was a lieutenant, first lieutenant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: First lieutenant. All right. Thank you very much. I apologise for interrupting you.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: As I said, I reported for duty at Pivka, and the commander of the company who was to give me my assignments was visibly surprised and was caught unawares with that kind of situation. He didn't expect to hand over his duties. His name was Jasmin Sahinovic. When I took over my duties, I spent my time in Pivka until July 1988, and at the time, there was a reorganisation, and my particular unit, including the 1st Battalion, was transferred from the Pivka garrison to the Postojna garrison, and together with my unit, I went into this new garrison, and I was there until the 12th of August, 1991. My duties as commander of the company, I gave over to the new commander, and he was Mr. Surkota, first lieutenant in Postojna. I think that that was in 1989, in February of that year, or perhaps in 1990. I took over my duties, I was the deputy commander of the 1st Battalion and, at the same time, assistant for matters of morale, and I performed those duties up until I left the Yugoslavia People's Army, that is to say, until I was no longer an active soldier. When I completed the military academy and graduated, we were given ranks by way of an automatic system, and so we all got our first rank on the 30th of July, 1983, and we were either lieutenants, we were all lieutenants, those were the ranks we were given, and those cadets who had gone to technical military academies were given the rank of first lieutenant. I obtained the rank of first lieutenant on the 30th of July, 1984, and this was also the next rank, that is to say, having spent one year as a lieutenant, I was promoted to a first lieutenant. Three years later, on the basis of assessments by my seniors, I was given the rank of captain on the 30th of July, 1987. Once again, I was professionally assessed on the 30th of July, 1990, and I received the rank of captain first class, and this was an extraordinary promotion, on the 22nd of December, 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please, what an extraordinary promotion means? What does this term mean in the Yugoslav People's Army? What is a regular promotion and this extraordinary early promotion?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, the difference was that you got a promotion after a shorter period of time, an early promotion, and the criteria for this promotion, which had to be fulfilled, were that the last two marks were excellent, with particular excellence, and those were the top marks given at that time within the armed forces of Yugoslavia. In my case, I was the commander of a company, and I had to have spent at least three years as commander of the company. I fulfilled that three-year time period, and this early promotion that I was granted for the most part was on the basis of my work results or as a stimulative measure. If anybody had scored any particular success, any officers.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So along with this purely military career of a career officer, you probably continued your education. Could you tell us something about that?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, at my first year at the military academy, I decided that I was going to do additional training and go on with my education, but there were a lot of extenuating circumstances so that I was not able to enrol in my studies at the beginning. We had to do field work in the course of my education and training. When I say "field work," this was outside the centres where the high military schools and academies were located. I told you of the places where I did my internship or training, but, in fact, what we did was we travelled throughout Yugoslavia, practically the whole of Yugoslavia, so I didn't have time, during my education at the military academy, to enrol in any other civilian studies. In 1987, I enrolled in postgraduate studies at the university in Banja Luka for business and legal informatics, that was the course I took, and in April 1989, I graduated, I completed my studies there, and sat for my oral examination for an MA, master's degree; however, I was not able to present my written topic because of the war conditions, so that I never received a diploma, although I have a certificate saying that I attended the four years of study and that I passed my oral examinations for my MA My intentions to further my education and to enrol at the faculty was, in a way, linked to what I planned to do, that is to say, I did not wish to continue my military career. A little beforehand, I had decided to leave active military service, but I was duty-bound to spend double the time that I had spent doing my education working as an active military man in the armed forces, and as I had spent six years doing my training and education, I had to spend 12 years working as a career military officer. After that, when I had completed those 12 years, I had gained the right to cease my military service, active military service.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, you were a successful career military officer. Why did you decide to become a civilian? What were your motives for making that decision?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: There were a number of reasons for this. Already since 1979 and onwards to 1980, there was a greater engagement and activation of the army on assignments, such as the Kosovo assignment. Later on, there was a reorganisation, that was implemented within the frameworks of the Yugoslav People's Army, and they indicated that individual cadres were being promoted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "individual cadres," you have in mind a certain ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do, so that there was an imbalance within the Yugoslav People's Army, the basic principle of unity or equality was being upset in this way, and already in 1985, this was particularly visible. All you had to do was to look at the commanding structure of any army, whichever army, and if you looked at the command and all the key posts, these were predominantly or, for the most part, uni-national in character.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell us which ethnic group became the dominant ethnic group at that time?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: According to criteria, that is to say, if you had a direct approach to this, the ethnic group was predominantly the Serbs, but not only the Serbs. There were Serbs from Bosnia-Herzegovina, from Serbia proper, and from all the areas of the former Yugoslavia. For example, in the battalion in which I served, the commander of the battalion was a Serb, and then the commanders of the companies were also predominantly Serbs. The commander of the brigade was also a Serb, as well as the chief of staff and a deputy commander, and the top commanding posts were almost uni-ethnic at that period, occupied by one ethnic group, and this, indeed, made me firmer in my resolve to stop being a career military man. In 1987, I tried, together with my parents and my in-laws, to open a business of my own which would employ some 40 workers, and we obtained all the necessary papers from the municipality of Cerknica in the Socialist Republic of Slovenia, and from the Postojna municipality, we got through all the red tape, but we needed a customs declaration for the import of the machinery that I was going to deal in, so I had to give up that project. The enrolment of my postgraduate studies, something that was paid for exclusively by my own family, that is to say, myself and my wife, was geared towards my future profession once I had left the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How long did you stay in the JNA? When did you actually decide that it was time for you to leave? Can you explain this to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I made a definite decision already at the end of June 1991 during the open conflicts that took place in the Republic of Slovenia; however, I, myself, like many of my colleagues, were there when the order was given by the chief of staff of the armed forces, which came sometime at the end of June and the beginning of July, which proclaimed a state of alert for us. A state of alert was proclaimed, and the decision was made that we could not avail ourselves of the rights and the rule of the governing armed service to cease military service, so that this order by the head of the general staff suspended our legal rights, and the order was in force until the end of July. Later on, it was withdrawn, and on the 12th of August, 1991, I tendered in my request for cessation of active military service, and on that same day, I left the Postojna garrison and left to -- in fact, I used the holiday that I had coming to me and the free days that I had earned during my military service, and I did not wait for an actual permit to reach me. I hoped that this would come in the next month or two, which is the amount of time that I had for my free days and my holiday, a dispensation from the army in written form.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Trial Chamber what the conflict in Slovenia was about?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: In Slovenia, there was a conflict between the Territorial Defence of the then first stage towards the creation of the armed forces of Slovenia and MUP on the one side; on the other hand, there were the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army. The first stage was the forces of the MUP. That is what they said they were. That's how they represented themselves. This conflict, for the most part, was linked to power and authority at the border crossings, who would be in control, and everything occurred after the assembly of Slovenia had made a decision to proclaim Slovenia a republic, that is to say, a sovereign independent and autonomous state in the territory of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At that time, therefore, when the conflict broke out between the JNA and, in all practical terms, the Slovenian people and their armed formations, you left. Is it true that you went to Vienna, Austria?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. Together with my wife -- my wife had left a little earlier, she had gone to Vienna before me, and I went to her sister, to my sister-in-law. She is an Austrian citizen. She has Austrian citizenship. My wife Ratka, her maiden name is Baresic, she is Baresic-Blaskic, she was born in 1970 in Austria, and she spent most of her time living with her parents in Austria and Germany. Her entire family, her mother still lives in Austria today, her parents live in Austria today, and so the two of us went to Vienna, and for the first month or so, we lived in an apartment owned by her sister. We had two rooms to ourselves there in that apartment, and after that month had elapsed, we managed to rent a small apartment for ourselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Please continue. What was your life in Austria like? Were you able to organise your life in Austria?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At the very beginning, my wife found employment. She finished her schooling in Austria, most of her education in Austria, and she knew the language well, and our son Dean was born in 1988, and he was staying with my in-laws, with his grandparents. At the beginning of 1992, he went to kindergarten in Austria. At that time, I spent most of my time studying the language, learning the language, and I also tendered in the documents necessary to obtain a work permit. I worked from time to time, and we succeeded in organising our life in Austria very quickly, particularly as we had good living conditions, and we had succeeded in transporting most of our effects and belongings to Austria and to furnish our apartment, which allowed us to live a decent life.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE SHAHABUDDEEN
utterances.text: Would it be convenient, in this sequence, for you to get the witness to put on the record when he got married, unless that has already been said?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Quite right, Your Honour. I was thinking of doing this in the course of the witness's testimony and wanted to interrupt him, but then I thought, let us leave it to the end, but this brings us to the decision to go to Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now I'd like to ask you, General, a little bit about your family life. When did you marry your present wife? When were your children born, the first child, your second child? Could you tell us a bit about your family life?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I married in 1987. I married Ratka Blaskic. She was born in 1970 in Austria. She is, by profession, a traffic technician and was not employed up until -- then she gave all her time to our family. We have two children. Asan Dean was born in 1988 in Postojna, the Socialist Republic of Slovenia, in July, and our second son, Ivan, was born in March 1996 in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: As we're talking about Ivan's birth, could you tell us the reason for which you came to The Hague on the 1st of April and not one or two months earlier when you heard about The Hague indictment?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, the reason was precisely because my wife had had a difficult pregnancy, and she had to be cared for by her physicians throughout her pregnancy, and I have the necessary documents on that score. Our first child, that is to say, our first child was not born because of that. She was pregnant, but she lost her first baby, and then both our next sons, Dean and Ivan, she was under the constant control of physicians. From November up until March, this was the time that I spent together with my wife taking her to medical examinations and check-ups during her pregnancy. In Zagreb, I think the hospital is called Petrova Hospital, it is the maternity department there. That is the basic reason why I did not come to The Hague immediately and place myself at the disposal of this Honourable Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So what you want to say is you did so as soon as your child was born?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. My wife left hospital on Monday morning, and on that particular Monday afternoon, I left for The Hague.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me take you back to your stay in Austria. You said that you were working on setting up conditions to live normally there, just like anywhere in western Europe, without particular stress or problems; however, you still decided to go to Bosnia where there was a war. Can you explain to the Trial Chamber your motives, why leave such a quiet, normal, regular life to go to Bosnia and Herzegovina and to this war which was about to begin, in fact, which had just begun? What were your motives?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: First of all, it is correct that I managed, along with my wife, and primarily thanks to her family and also her own knowledge of language, we managed to secure a fairly decent and, I could say, pleasant lifestyle, at least as comfortable as it was in the former Yugoslavia; however, my own parents remained back in that area. When I say "that area," I mean Bosnia and Herzegovina, so my parents and relatives were there. Then I was also aware of the fact that similar destruction may visit Bosnia and Herzegovina, just as it did Slovenia and Croatia. I received a number of calls, both from my relatives and from the representatives of the authorities in Kiseljak, and my basic motivation was that I felt a moral obligation to assist, and I knew and I was aware of the fact that I had the requisite expertise and that I could help prepare the defence against the aggression with which Bosnia was threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Now, who threatened Bosnia? Who was your potential enemy?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was obvious when the JNA forces were transferred, that is, what we called the "crack" forces, the majority of this force was transferred to Bosnia and Herzegovina. The same was done with large numbers of troops which were being transferred from the Republic of Croatia. What may not have been as apparent, at least not publicly, was a huge amount of materiel which was also being transferred to some larger centres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "materiel," can you clarify that because I think that you're about to use it quite a bit?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I mean the ammunition of all kinds, ordinance, artillery, infantry, and so on, explosives, mines, so combat materiel, then spare parts and everything else that a military formation can use in order to be effective and to have the maximum power, including armaments.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you reached this decision in Austria to go back, was it very clear to you that there would be a bloody conflict between the JNA and people in Bosnia and Herzegovina, primarily the Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: For a long time, I had a dilemma what to do. It was clear to me that the conflict would take place, but I could not even imagine that it would be of such proportions. I expected a conflict to happen and I expected some combat, but when I talked to my wife about it and when I told her about this option to go, she disagreed. She believed that we were to seek our future in the country where she was born. So this decision of -- I delayed my decision until late March of 1992 when, in a conversation with an official from the municipal crisis staff, I agreed to come and set one condition only, which was that my involvement be temporary and that it last no more than two months.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just to clarify. Can you define -- did you imagine that the parties to the conflict would be Bosnia and Herzegovina, regardless of the length or the size of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I believed that on the one side there would be the Yugoslav People's Army, regardless of how it may be transformed and what name it may assume, because the other side was already left without arms and without equipment due to the orders issued by the supreme command to transfer all the arms belonging to the Territorial Defence to the JNA. So, on the other side, I thought that it would be Croats and Bosnian Muslims in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that you received a call from the municipal crisis staff. Could you say from which municipal crisis staff, from which person, and when you left for Bosnia and Herzegovina and what happened during your journey?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: It was not a single call that I received, they came continuously, and so as I kept prolonging my decision, I received a number of calls by Mr. Pero Madzar on behalf of the municipal crisis staff, this is how he introduced himself, and after I reached my --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What town?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was this the town where you were born?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this is the municipality where I was born and this is my hometown. So this also contributed to my decision to go back and help my hometown.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. Now we are moving towards Bosnia and Herzegovina. This may be a good time to break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. The afternoon is long. We are going to take our first break, and we will return in 15 or 20 minutes. As regards the arrangements here, things are going to change a little bit. Be sure that the accused/witness be taken to the location which is appropriate to him. However, when the Court returns, we would like the witness to be in the courtroom. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will now resume the hearing. Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo, you may continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: We left off at your decision to go back to Bosnia and Herzegovina and to take over one of the military duties in the defence of Kiseljak for two months. However, your trip to Kiseljak did not run as smoothly as expected, so can you tell the Trial Chamber what happened and put it in a time frame, please?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I left on 5th April from Vienna via Zagreb to Kiseljak. In Zagreb, I spent the night. I used the opportunity to visit my brother on the evening of the 5th. On the 6th, in the morning, I also stayed with my brother in the Slava Raskaj school centre in Zagreb, and then along with him and another friend, we took the Podrevska highway via Bosanski Samac to Kiseljak. This road was a longer one than usual. There were a number of checkpoints on this road, both through Croatia and through Bosnia and Herzegovina. At one of these checkpoints, somewhere between 14.00 and 15.00 hours in the afternoon on the 6th, we were stopped by the reserve police force of the Bosnian MUP. These police were Serbs; I could gather that from the dialect and also by the fact that they were deployed in the immediate vicinity of the military police forces of the JNA. They searched our vehicle, and in the driver's side door, they found a small handgun, and in the driver's pocket, they found prayer beads. The policeman asked the driver whether he had a permit for the handgun, and the driver said, since this was a small-calibre handgun, he believed that he did not need one. After this, we were detained to an elementary school building, and there was a sign over the entrance of the elementary school which helped me locate the place, but it was Podhovlje near Doboj. I had never been there before. There we were questioned, our IDs were thoroughly checked, and we were even physically mistreated to a degree until 21.00 hours. Then, at 21.00 hours, we were placed into the APCs of the military police, and we were transferred to the Doboj barracks belonging to the JNA. There the questioning was resumed until late into the night, and that night we spent in the military detention unit which was part of this garrison. The next morning, myself and my friend, whose name was Mladen Coric, who drove me, were transferred to the Tuzla garrison. This was the headquarters of the Tuzla corps of the JNA. The barracks where we were brought were called the Husinjski Miners' barracks which I was able again to identify by the sign over the gate. I also had never been there before. I spent a period until the 13th of April there, and there I was again subjected to questioning, and we were accused of a number of things, including that I had deserted the former JNA, that I had worked for some intelligence agency in the West because I also had a German dictionary on me and a notebook in which I made notes. On the 13th of April, we were told that we would be exchanged for some people in prison in Mitrovica, and in the early afternoon, we were released from the garrison. We did not go to be exchanged in Sremska Mitrovica, and we only had problems in retrieving the documents which would allow us -- the car documents which would allow us to continue the journey. But later on we were able to retrieve the documents because the JNA forces were there in this garrison which earlier had been stationed in Postojna, so in a way, these were acquaintances of mine. These were people who knew me. From the Tuzla garrison, we left there at around 9.00 p.m. and went through Tuzla. Again, we went to Doboj and we were searched. At different checkpoints, we were searched all the way through until we left to Zenica. We wanted to reach Busovaca, but members of the MUP reserve forces, that is, the Bosnian MUP reserve forces, told us -- this was in Drivusa, that the road was closed and that we could only use the road Kakanj-Visoko-Kiseljak. So this is the road that we too, and after midnight sometime on the 14th of April, 1992, we finally reached our destination.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Very well. So you reached Kiseljak on the 14th of April, 1992. Tell me, who did you report to, what conversations did you have, and what was your understanding of the situation there?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: On 14 April, sometime in the afternoon, I reported to the president of the Kiseljak municipality, Josip Boro. This is the first time that we met. Until that time, I had never been to the president's office, and I did not know about these political structures because I had been gone since '85. I would only come back briefly during vacation. He briefed me on the situation in this area and let me know that he expected my arrival and that now he was on duty as the president of the municipal crisis staff and that the municipal assembly had seized its work. In its last session, it appointed the municipal crisis staff in which both Muslims and Croats equally participated and that this crisis staff took over all civilian and military affairs in the territory of the Kiseljak municipality. I let him know that I did not intend to stay beyond those two months but that I was willing, in the period of those two months, to provide my expert experience in order to prepare the territory and men to defend the territory against the attacks of the forces of Republika Srpska and that I believed that those two months should be enough to organise the defence in this area. I stressed that I did not expect any remuneration, any compensation, and that my driver was going to be a relative of mine, and so I therefore did not even need a vehicle or any other benefits or privileges. Several days later, I had an opportunity to attend certain meetings of the municipal crisis staff, even though I never was a member of the Kiseljak municipal crisis staff. What I noticed was that the military structure of this military crisis staff was very vague. A member of the municipal staff was the president of the People's Defence Affairs department, which was a civilian function, and it was Mr. Vojislav (sic) Trutina who was on this duty, and there was also the commander of the Territorial Defence staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tomislav is the name. This was a misspelling.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, his name was Tomislav Trutina. So the other part of this military body was the command, and that is the commander of the Territorial Defence staff of Kiseljak, Sead Sinahbasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He was a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was a Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And Tomislav Trutina is a Croat?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: That is correct. The joint command was also part of this military political body, and as early as late April, I was on duty as the commander of the armed forces for the Kiseljak municipality on behalf of the Croatian community, and along with me, the commander of the armed forces of Kiseljak municipality was Bakir Alispahic on behalf of the Muslim community.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to this undefined military structure, what was your perception of this municipal structure? Were they somehow linked to the higher authority within the republic?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, it was not linked to some higher governing body. In fact, the municipality sort of kept all its previous functions and also, because of the situation that existed, it also took over some prerogatives of a state, so that it was, in a way, a mini-state, which was a state within the boundaries of the municipality territory. All the problems which were dictated by this current situation were resolved, or at least attempted to be resolved, at the level of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So in addition to this municipal government which had both political and military aspects, what were the additional military formations which you found in the territory of the municipality at the time when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I expected to find certain formations, that is, the Territorial Defence formations there, or something similar, something that would be similar to what the case was in the Republic of Slovenia. However, in the territory of Kiseljak municipality, after a short while, I was able to see that there were villages which were armed and where the inhabitants had, in different ways, acquired weapons. Further, there were private units where some of the wealthier persons in the municipality had armed their own units, some of which were to protect their property from the criminal gangs which were operating in the area. In short, there were some private units. Then there were groups of hunters, people who already had legally-acquired weapons from before and who organised themselves. I also noticed, at the level of villages again, that they all had a great degree of autonomy. Their commanders or representatives were, in fact, sort of mouthpieces of positions that the villagers had taken and not part of any military structure in the villages. In addition to these village forces, there were nine civilian police stations which had been mobilised in case of war. They had 25 to 50 reserve policemen each, and there were nine of these reserve police stations. In addition, there were MUP forces, which was the civilian police station in Kiseljak. Then there were the Patriotic League forces which had their headquarters at one time at the Hotel Dalmatia in Kiseljak and later on in the elementary school in the town of Kiseljak. Further, there were Territorial Defence units. In Lepenica, there were small groups of Black Swans. There were also groups or units of HOS. This was in the town of Kiseljak and in the local commune of Lepenica. Then there were groups of HVO. Further, groups of armed displaced persons or refugees which had passed through Kiseljak, Kiseljak being one of the points of transit, and then there were the JNA units, that is, from before. There was an artillery battalion stationed there which had high artillery power, 128-millimetre guns, and a military police company which had been transferred from the Marshall Tito barracks in Zagreb to the Kiseljak barracks. There were also crews of the radio relay in Cubren. They also belonged to the former JNA. In short, there were a number of armed groups in a relatively small area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Tell us, please. You said that there were many armed groups. What was the basic characteristic of those groups and what did you do in that situation? Did you succeed in imposing yourself on these groups or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The basic characteristic and activity of these groups, with the exception of the forces of the Yugoslav People's Army which were still present in the municipality of Kiseljak, they would parade around brandishing their weapons and uniforms, they would go around the centre of town. Those groups which were nearer to the main roads of communication also engaged in setting up barricades, roadblocks, or checkpoints in order to ensure material benefit from them. I, myself, was not accepted by those groups, they did not accept me as their commander, except when they needed my professional aid and assistance. So from time to time, I was able to function as a commander when my skills and expertise were needed, but it was very difficult to ensure any genuine authority over them, and I had the impression that I would need a great deal of time to deserve this right and to ask them to heed my orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In a situation of this kind, which was not the usual type of army relationship according to your experience and what you were used to up until then, what methods of work were you able to apply? Were you able to apply what you learnt previously with regard to command or did you have to apply any other methods, and, if so, describe, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, what methods you applied?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, quite right, I was not able to apply the doctrine of command that I had been taught because I did not have the subordinate elements in the chain of command. Let me explain this with an example of villages. If, for example, a village had 25 recruits, then it would have one representative who would be replaced several times a day, depending on how successful he was in representing the interests of the village. If the village was one that had 200 inhabitants, once again, it would have just one representative, and I, as the commander -- what happened once was that one of these villages would call me to attend the meeting at which they would elect their commander and relieve him of his duty, and I would be told in advance that I did not have the right of decision making or taking part in the discussion and that all I could do was to be there in the capacity of a guest, and this happened to me in the village of Lepenica in the Kiseljak area. In the command structure, there were different types of weapons. Generally, there were different calibre and small arms, some of them that dated back to the Second World War, others that had been manufactured by hand, hand-crafted weapons, but, for the most part, I applied three types of methods in my work, and I was fully conscious of the fact that I could not expect my commanding to be effective, and I decided to hold oral lectures and to convince people, by speaking to them and by convincing the formal or informal leaders of the different villages, and I differentiated between the two, and I also would select representatives from the individual villages, and I would go with them on visits to the positions that I thought were crucial and that we should visit in order to set up a defence line.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Before you go on to explain how you set up your defence lines, could you tell us, who were you defending the Kiseljak municipality from? Who did you expect to attack the territory of the Kiseljak municipality?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: We organised a defence for the municipality of Kiseljak, a defence against the forces of what was still the Yugoslav army and which later became the army of the Republika Srpska from the Ilidza municipality and area, because in April, there had already been attacks by these forces in the Rakovica area, which is the first village bordering on the Kiseljak municipality, the first neighbouring place from which about 300 Muslim Bosniaks were expelled. This was the first large influx of displaced persons at the time who were taken into the Kiseljak area, so we defended the municipality of Kiseljak from the attacks by the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Would you explain to the Court what your work, in fact, comprised, your work with the representatives of the villages or these armed individuals from the villages? What did you, in fact, discuss with them?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Usually in the mornings, together with Bakir --

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who is Bakir?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Bakir Alispahic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He was the Muslim commander, was he not?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, he was. He was the Muslim commander who I met with daily. I had a daily meeting with him, a briefing, and we would decide which one of us would go to which village. They were villages bordering on the Lepenica and Brnjaci area, and, Mr. President and Your Honours, if necessary, I can show you on this relief here.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: It will be much clearer, I think, if you do so. Could you show us the defence lines and where you expected the attacks to be launched?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Can the cameras focus on the model so that the people in the public gallery can follow?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: And microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You can approach. It's a little complicated because the Judges have to be able to see, the public gallery has to be able to see, the witness has to be able to express himself, and the parties have to be able to supervise. We have to try to organise things. I think at the beginning we were able to do that with the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARMON
utterances.text: Mr. President, perhaps it would be helpful if we have multiple jacks installed over here for the benefit of all counsel to approach this. It's difficult for us to see. There's only one jack over here. We can't understand Colonel Blaskic without translation, and from this distance, we can't approach the exhibit without translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Yes. I have no problem with that, but, of course, when you're all around the model, the only ones who won't be able to see will be the Judges. Well, let's try. All right. Approach the model.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: General, perhaps, for the beginning, it would be a good idea to tell us where the larger towns are located on this model.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I am pointing to Kiseljak (indicating). That is the place where I arrived on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Okay. We can see very clearly. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I arrived there on the 14th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: Where are we in relation to the map that I have? Can you show us?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This is north (indicating). Your Honours, north is towards this point (indicating). That is north.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. Continue, please.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, Kiseljak, where I arrived on the 14th of April, 1992, is located here (indicating). My work throughout the entire time, that is to say, in April and May, took place in the area around Kokoska, the Kokoska facility. This is the range, mountain range, north of the main road running from Kiseljak to Rakovica, Ilidza, and on to Sarajevo. Sarajevo is in that direction (indicating). Then we have the Kobiljaca mountain pass, and the position here is the trigonometry reference 651 or the high ground referred to by the figure 651. Then we have the Pljesevac feature, and this whole feature is called Besovac. This pass between the Pljesevac feature is called Ravne Njive. I'm indicating Ravne Njive (indicating) and the feature Ostrik. To the right of the feature Ostrik, we have the mountain range which is called Koscan. This is where the forces of the Territorial Defence from the Kiseljak municipality were located. On the Ostrik feature, Pljesevac and the Kobiljaca pass with the 651 high ground feature and Kokoska, these were the HVO forces. Further on, we have the forces of the Territorial Defence of Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You have now described the frontline towards the Serbs. Tell us, please, in simplified terms for layman purposes, what was your activity in these mountain ranges, features, passes, and so on? What did you teach the locals there?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I would go to these villages every day. They are villages bordering on this area. They are the village of Azapovici, Dugandzica Kuce. They are the bordering villages along this line here, and I would select or I would pinpoint the leaders of these villages, and together with them, I would go on foot every day and visit these positions, Ostrik, Pljesevac, Kobiljaca, Kokoska, and would show the locals, the local villagers, where to dig trenches and fortifications, communicating trenches, and other types of fortification and, in the engineering sense, how to set up the frontlines, the defence lines. Having shown them where this work to fortify the lines should be done, I would move on to another area to check and see whether what I had ordered had been carried out, and this was repeated time and again over a long period of time because they were slow in undertaking this kind of work. Nobody was actually delighted in having to go trench digging.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: This defence line, was it a mixed Croat-Muslim defence line, and did you work both together with the Muslims and Croats? How was this work organised?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have already stated that the Koscan position and Mokrine and further on were held by the forces of the Territorial Defence from Kiseljak and Hadzici and, from time to time, manned by people from Jablanica as well. From Koscan feature on towards the villages of Kralupi, Godusa, those were forces belonging to the Territorial Defence of Visoko. I toured all these villages, and, in fact, at the beginning, I wasn't interested in which village was Croatian and which was Muslim, unless I was told this expressly by the locals. At the beginning, I would go to Zabrdje, Brkovica, Mokrine, to Tulica, and also to the village of Grahovci, and I toured all these positions in the area, and I never differentiated between the villages and distinguished between the Croatian villages and Muslim villages, but I would check these lines and, together with the locals and the villagers, I would explain how, in engineering terms, this terrain should be organised for defence purposes. I already said that Bakir and myself, that is to say, Bakir suggested to me or I would suggest to Bakir, we would go together to visit some of the villages, so that we would make a public display for the villages and show them that we were not divided, regardless of the fact that, conditionally speaking, we had HVO positions here and TO positions there, and from Kokoska to the River Bosna, we, once again, had the Territorial Defence forces of Visoko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In addition to determining the defence lines and positions and the engineering terms of organisation, did you try to tell the villagers the importance of training, and did you explain the ways in which the Republika Srpska could attack and how to defend against these attacks?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, during my training at the military academy, I underwent tactical drills at company level on the Rakovica position, and we would elaborate defence plans towards Sarajevo, a defence set up to an enemy attacking the Lepenica valley towards Sarajevo. Using the knowledge and experience that I had gained and the experience gained from tactical courses and activities within the JNA, I, together with the representatives of the villages, toured some of the positions and tried to explain to them -- first, I would do this orally, and I'd explain the stages of attack that the army of the Republika Srpska would undertake and what we can expect, the kind of tactics we could expect from them, and what we should do in retaliation. Together with them, I would set up reserve posts and positions which were, for the most part, on the slopes of Cubrena and above the villages in the Lepenica valley. In addition to work of this kind, I also endeavoured to organise training courses, that is, basic training teaching the people how to handle weapons, the kind of weapons that they had, the armed peasants and villagers, basics in weapons handling, but there were a great deal of problems there because sometimes ten people would have ten different types of weapons. The other problem was that each individual thought he was trained in the handling and manipulation of weapons just because he knew how to place ammunition, how to charge the weapon, how to load the weapon. I would also go to the individual villages, usually in the afternoon hours or towards the evening, and I would have discussions and talks with the locals, and I would try and convince them that all these preparatory measures were a good thing and should be done because I tried to bear upon them that organisation was a good thing, particularly with the winter advancing in these mountain regions, and the winter is very harsh in these areas, and so we should try and predict the intentions of the enemy and the army of the Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that some of the villages in these border areas next to the frontline, that some of the villages were Muslim villages and others were Croatian villages. What about the TO, was it completely Muslim or mixed? What about the HVO, was it an expression of Croatian military organisation?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: To a certain extent, the majority, yes, although both in the HVO, there were some Bosniak Muslims, and the complete composition of the Patriotic League within the HVO, yes, they were Bosniak Muslims. We had certain difficulties in that respect because certain members of the Territorial Defence expressed their readiness to join the HVO, which sometimes meant the possibility of avoiding any kind of responsibility, and this is what happened amongst the HVO ranks as well. For example, for one week, people would be members of the HVO, and the next week, something else, depending on what the responsibility and duty was.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Apart from these exceptions, generally speaking, can we say that the Territorial Defence was an organisation of the Bosniak people and the HVO was an organisation of the Croats?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was true, except the exceptions which occurred, for the most part, when operations to deblock Sarajevo were launched and which were the result of the fact that the TO had lost its membership, but the TO was Bosniak Muslim, and the HVO was made up of Croatian recruits.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Perhaps, General, you can go back to your seat and we can continue from there. Therefore, your activity was the organisation of a defence line. Who saw to the safety and security of the territory in-depth, that is, the security of the people living there and their property in the municipality of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I have already said that the municipality had nine wartime police stations of a reserve police force. These police stations were set up, as far as I know, already in 1991, at the end of 1991, in fact; and, together with the active formation of the civilian police force, they were in charge of public law and order and safety and security throughout the territory of Kiseljak. They were well-armed at the time, and they set up checkpoints in front of their wartime police stations, for the most part, which were located on the main roads leading towards the Kiseljak municipality, into the municipality from the local communities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can we say, therefore, that the civilian police was in charge of security throughout the territory?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Well, yes, it had complete control of security throughout the territory, all the more so as the fact that the commander of the civilian police station, the chief of civilian police, by virtue of his function, was included, was a member of the municipal crisis staff, that is, he was a member of the civilian and military authorities at the municipal level, and this structure of the police station was very well-balanced. When I say "well-balanced," I mean that the commander, the chief, was a Croat, his deputy was a Muslim Bosniak; the commander of the police station, the civilian police station in Kiseljak was a Muslim Bosniak, his deputy was a Croat; and it was their task to control the territory behind the frontline in the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Was there civilian protection? If there was, was it unified, and what was the civilian protection like at the time when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Immediately upon my arrival, maybe a week later, this would be around the 26th of April, the JNA air force, or the air force of the Republika Srpska, bombed Busovaca, and several days before, there were flyovers, even though they did not drop any bombs. At that time, I asked whether any measures had been taken, and I asked to meet with the person in charge of the civilian protection to discuss the measures for protection of the civilian population. So I met with the commander and the chief of the civilian protection. At that time, we agreed that the shelters should be marked clearly again and some other measures. The civilian protection in these circumstances was trying to be operational to the extent that it was possible. However, I recall very well this meeting with the commander of the civilian protection for two reasons: When I first asked him, I was interested to know where the evacuation routes were for the civilians in case of attack, and he said that it was in the direction of Ilidza, that is down the Lepenica valley, which would be from Kiseljak towards the frontline. So the civilians would be evacuated towards the frontlines. And I told him that this was not right at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you just slow down, please?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This would mean that the evacuation is being conducted towards the frontlines, and he said that these actions were set down in the rules, in the handbook which he received, and that he could not change it until such change was agreed to by his superior at the republican level. We found a compromise so that he would not change the rules in the handbook but that the evacuation would not be conducted towards the frontline. The second issue was the distribution of duties for the civilian protection between the HVO and the TO. I gave him my position, that there is no need for such a distribution of duty because the entire population should be covered in the territory of the Kiseljak municipality, including both sides; that is, both Muslims and Croats and members of other ethnic groups and minorities which lived in the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So in conclusion, before we move on to the next area: If you were to sum up the methods which you used, did you operate as a military commander in relation to soldiers or was it something else? How would you qualify this?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No. In fact, I suspected and I sincerely hoped that I would find some kind of military structure in place there, but in reality, what I found were armed groups, and these working men and these villagers I perceived as men who had taken up arms, who had put on uniforms and who were prepared to, instead of going to the factory, would be prepared to play a role given them. I was not in a position to issue any orders and expect that somebody among my direct subordinates would carry them out because I did not have any kind of a structure upon which I could rely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So there was not a structure established in the downward sense, in a subordinate way, but how was the military structure upwards, so to speak; in other words, were there any superiors to you at the HVO level?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At the session of the municipal crisis staff around the 23rd of April, 1992, I was appointed the commander of the armed formations by the municipal crisis staff in Kiseljak, and I was not, either in the first contact or later, led to believe that there was a military structure superior to the municipality from which I was to seek either approval or which was to verify this appointment of mine. Also, as far as my work is concerned, I never was aware of any superior structure, something that I could relate to my previous work, in other words, an entity to which I would report on my daily activities. I would only occasionally inform members of the municipal crisis staff in Kiseljak on my activities or members of the HVO headquarters in Kiseljak, and there was no superior military structure in existence at the time above this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When and in what way did you meet someone who at least theoretically may have been your superior?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, sometime in early May 1992, around the 5th of May, the commander of the municipal headquarters of the HVO, Tomislav Trutina, proposed that I accompany him on a trip to Busovaca on a fact-finding mission, that I accompany him during this trip. I went along, and we arrived at Motel Tisa, which is on the approaches to town, and here in this motel I met and I greeted Mr. Pasko Ljubicic, and we had an informal conversation which lasted for several minutes. This was at the reception desk in the motel. And then I sat down with Tomo in a restaurant. We sat down at a table.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you tell me what you were told? What was Pasko Ljubicic's post?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: At that time, Tomo told me, "Here, you see this man? This is Pasko. He's the commander of the regional headquarters of the HVO for Central Bosnia." We sat down in this restaurant. Pasko, for a while, went away to make some telephone calls, and we were joined by a gentleman, whom I later learned that his name was Filip Filipovic and he used to be a colonel in the former JNA, and Lieutenant-Colonel Filipovic briefly gave us his impressions about the operation at Slimena. This was an operation in which the HVO forces were involved. I'm not sure whether the TO was also involved in it. This was in the territory of Travnik municipality where a warehouse was surrounded with the weapons of the Territorial Defence for the municipalities of Busovaca, Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Zenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When you say "Territorial Defence," was this the Muslim Territorial Defence or the Territorial Defence which was still under the JNA control?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, what I am referring to is the Territorial Defence which was part of the structure of the armed forces of the former Yugoslavia; in other words, under the control of the Yugoslav People's Army, not -- I do not refer to the Territorial Defence established by the leadership of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How were the weapons distributed?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I did not review the documents to see how the weapons were distributed except there, at the restaurant, I listened to what Filipovic was saying, and he pointed out that about 75 per cent of the weapons ended up in the hands of Bosniak Muslims and about -- that is, of the total weapons -- 25 per cent went to the Croats. He also said that the HVO members had casualties during this operation, there were both killed and wounded, but he also said that he managed to reach an agreement with the TO representatives and that this distribution was to be balanced approximately 50-50 per cent. However, he told us that he had agreed to this distribution.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Can you tell me about this meeting? Did you receive any instructions, any orders, either by Pasko Ljubicic or Filip Filipovic?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No. I was surprised at that time because I had expected that the meeting was about to start and that this discussion could have been an expose by Colonel Filipovic. It was just kind of a briefing to let us know what had happened. However, at one point, the commander, Tomislav Trutina, told me that it was time for us to start going back, and so we returned to Kiseljak without any orders, information, or any kind of military report. This is how my first contact with these, let's call it "formerly superior officers," ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me just sum up. Pasko Ljubicic was formerly your first commander, and this is the same Pasko Ljubicic who was to be the commander of the military police in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Could you now describe the next meeting which you had with superiors at the HVO?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The next meeting was sometime towards the end of May of '95. I think that, more precisely, it was on the 23rd of May, 1992. My commander, Tomislav Trutina, and I again left Kiseljak en route to Busovaca. I know that we were supposed to see whether they had any anti-armour weapons because there was a threat of a tank attack against Kiseljak. In a motel, and I believe it's called Villa Titovac in Busovaca, I met a brigadier who introduced himself as Brigadier Zarko Tole. He was accompanied by two uniformed men, one was his driver and the other one was probably his escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: What was Zarko Tole's duty?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I only know that he told me, when he introduced himself, that he was the commander of the regional headquarters for -- regional staff for Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Just one more comment. Does that mean that Zarko Tole had meanwhile replaced Pasko Ljubicic?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that would have meant that we had a new commander, that Zarko Tole was a new commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. I suggest that we take a 15-minute break and then we'll resume at 4.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: We will resume the hearing now. Please be seated. Mr. Nobilo?

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: At the break, we left off when you, sometime on the 23rd of May, arrived at a meeting with the HVO staff commander and you realised that there was a new commander in place, Mr. Tole. Could you describe your conversation with him a little bit?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. This was a new commander whom I met for the first time that afternoon, and he informed us on the events mostly focusing on the Kupres front and on the probable intentions of the army of Republika Srpska in the area of Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, Prozor, Tomislavgrad, and Novi Travnik, Travnik, and Jajce.
