However, he also said that on that day, at 19.00 hours, a meeting was set up with the civilian and military authorities in the Busovaca municipality conference room and that it would be good if we also attended this meeting. He stressed that this meeting, which was to be held in the Busovaca municipality building, will be attended by representatives of both the Muslim and Croatian communities. Tomislav Trutina and I stayed on for that meeting, and in this meeting, Commander Tole spoke for the most part, and he described his own view of the military situation and he said that the representatives of both the Croatian and Muslim communities in Busovaca municipality should overcome certain disagreements and differences and that they should focus their forces for the defence against the upcoming attacks by the army of the Republika Srpska. He particularly emphasised the need for a joint defence and informed us that a joint command had already been established which was focusing on the developments on the Kupres front. However, this meeting too ended up without any firm orders for us by this new commander except for the usual military information, that was the standard military information that was given about the current situation. Nothing else was given. He also stated that a meeting had been held in Travnik with representatives of the Croatian and Muslim communities, and as far as I can recall, it may also have been held in Vitez and perhaps in Novi Travnik. After this meeting, I returned to the municipal headquarters in Kiseljak and continued my daily activities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did you receive any combat order from your superior commander Tole?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No. Apart from this information, this briefing, which really dealt with how he saw the role of the civilian representatives in terms of assistance, logistics, and everything else relating to the defence and creating a line of defence in Central Bosnia, at no point did he issue any kind of task or order, nor did I receive any from him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: When did you next meet with your commander?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The next meeting, and then this was again a new commander for the regional headquarters for Central Bosnia, was on the 5th of June, 1992 in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Who was the commander at the time? This was a new commander or was this the old commander Tole?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I think it was translated "the 5th of June," and it's come out "the 15th of June." I don't know, in terms of the testimony, if that's of any consequence, but for accuracy's sake, I point that out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The 5th of June, the 5th; is that correct, General?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the meeting was held on the 5th of June. Who was there? Who was now the commander of this regional headquarters for Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, we assembled for this meeting a little bit early on that occasion, and again we met with our now new commander. This was a commander who introduced himself as Zulu. He did not give us his full name, and I assumed that this was his nom de guerre. In this meeting, Commander Zulu, after he introduced himself as the new commander of the regional headquarters for Central Bosnia, informed us again about the current events on the Kupres front, predominantly, the development in the Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, Novi Travnik, and Jajce areas, and this meeting was suddenly interrupted by the arrival of a soldier who brought a message to the commander. Fifteen to twenty minutes later, we learned the reason for this interruption, and the commander told us only that he, himself, was calling the next meeting for the 9th of June, 1992, again in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Did this new commander issue you any orders or did he establish a chain of command, a chain of subordination?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, he did not. He did not issue any orders. He didn't even ask us to give him our names so that he would know who attended this meeting and which commanders attended. He, in no way, issued any orders, let alone any combat orders. This was a very brief meeting, and it consisted only of his speech about what he thought was going on. There was a big difference between the briefing of the previous commander Tole and Commander Zulu.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let us leave aside for the moment your contacts with your immediate superiors, until the time when you, yourself, became the superior officer there. Could you just give us, very briefly, your comments on the civilian authorities in Kiseljak, how you saw them after two or three months of being there?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, my arrival in Kiseljak and my reporting to the local civilian authorities was my first direct contact with the civilian authorities. As a cadet during my military training and later on as a professional officer, I lived in a system which was completely insulated from the civilian government. Only when I needed to report my residence, which was in Postojna and Ljubljana, did I have any dealings with any civilian authorities, and the former JNA had all other services militarised. I realised that the supreme power in the Kiseljak municipality was held by the municipal crisis staff and that all of the military and civilian governing was issued from there. The civilian authorities at that time tried to keep their former authority, but, in my view, it was also forced to take over all other functions, state functions, which was due to the fact that the state had ceased to function there. The municipal crisis staff mostly worked through joint meetings, sessions, which included representatives of both Croatian and Bosniak Muslim communities. What I noticed in these meetings was that there was no agenda or prepared plan of what the discussion was about, but certain events in the Kiseljak municipality dictated the agenda of these meetings, and usually this municipal authority, for the most part, reacted like some kind of fire fighting crew. If a fire broke out somewhere, that is, if certain incidents or events happened, then they would respond. The decisions were taken by consensus, by mutual agreement, or by voting. When voting, the Croats had the relative majority, and frequently the decisions which were adopted by vote were not agreed to by the Bosniak Muslim side. They often had objections to the rules, and I know that the rules were set up by their local municipal assembly. Apart from these types of decision taking, I never noticed any superior civilian government bodies or any form of coordination between the higher civilian government bodies. I remember, for instance, the issue of food supplies, when there were shortages, a municipal commission was established but only after the shortages were already present and when a need arose to find ways to find new supplies. At that time, humanitarian aid was not yet in place, but we had a problem with the influx of refugees.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Let me move on to another area, and let me move to the period of time until you became the commander of the Operative Zone. As regards the incidents in Kiseljak municipality, I'm talking about the period of summer, that is, June/July of 1992 and on, was this a period of peace? Were there any armed conflicts? Could you describe the situation a little bit and then maybe try to give us some of the incidents and how it was related later on to the armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the disintegration of the state and the fact that the state structures ceased to function, coupled with the lack of authority, there was no power and authority, and voluntary armament in the area of Kiseljak, as well as the breakdown generally of law and order and the movement of armed groups in the Kiseljak area, brought about a very unstable situation which was very often accompanied by incidents of various kinds. What I noticed at the very beginning of this period was that the incidents generally occurred in the villages, that is to say, not in the structure of municipal power and authority and in the municipal headquarters, but in the villages, first and foremost, and they were motivated, principally, for economic and social reasons. Regardless of these motives, each of the incidents, and there were many of them, had an effect on the population of Kiseljak, and that effect was that the population was afraid and distrustful. Very often, they would react on their own behalf, and if the complicating parties happened to be the members of different ethnic groups, then this would deepen the fear and mistrust that already existed and create a basis for the generation of new incidents. It was enough for somebody to know that an activity or operation would take place to trigger off a broader incident. It was enough to learn of the movement of troops from outside or the movement of armed groups; this too would trigger off an incident of some kind. Sometimes the reasons for certain reactions were perhaps justified, sometimes they were unjustified, but the effect of any incident and all incidents was to widen the gap and increase the fear and mistrust and to have people polarise, the members of the Croatian ethnic group and the members of the Bosniak Muslims. Generally speaking, what could be perceived was that these incidents did take place, and they were incidents between the members of the HVO and HOS, between the members of the Territorial Defence and the Patriotic League, and also between the armed villagers from the neighbouring Croatian villages, that is to say, one Croatian village against another Croatian village. Then there would be conflicts between the members of the armed locals of the Bosniak Muslim villages and Croatian villages; furthermore, between the members of the Serbian villages and the Bosniak Muslim villages. There were also incidents between the members of the armed villagers, who were Croats and Muslim Bosniaks, directed against the reserve unit of the civilian police which was mobilised in nine local communities. There were also incidents between the members of the military police and the civilian police force. There were also incidents at that time between armed groups which sold weapons and engaged in other activities, usually the black market, a type of black marketing. There were also incidents when troops were brought in from outside, units which, according to somebody's plan, suddenly arrived and worked according to their own plans in the Kiseljak area without being previously announced.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Having described the situation, could you tell us about some of the incidents that occurred in May or June 1992 for us to be able to support your assessments with facts?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I am going to quote an incident which occurred on the 3rd of May, 1992 at the very exit to the Kiseljak municipality, that is, as you leave the Kiseljak municipality, a motorised column was formed comprising of ten motor vehicles, members of HOS, in the late evening hours, and this column moved from the Kiseljak municipality towards the Brnjaci local community and on towards Lepenica. While they were driving, they opened automatic gunfire using small arms. The route was 10 to 12 kilometres, and this created enormous problems for us because the locals from these two local communities, that is to say, both the Croats and the Muslims and the Serbs who lived in the Kiseljak municipality, thought that the army of the Republika Srpska had carried out an attack and taken control of those two local communities, and the rest of the night we spent trying to establish what had, in fact, occurred, and we did our best to calm the situation and bring things back to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you recall a convoy from Foca escorted by the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina and the alarm that that created in the town of Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The next incident, that is to say, after the incident of the 3rd of May, I myself and the commander, that is to say, Commander Bakir, were invited to attend a meeting of the municipal crisis staff to submit reports on what had happened; and on the 4th of May, 1992, in the afternoon, I left for the meeting together with Bakir. However, he asked the driver to take him to the crossroads, this is the junction, at this position (indicating), and I was surprised why he wanted to be taken to the crossroads because we had this meeting of the municipal crisis staff where we were expected to table a report on the events of the previous night and the incident that had taken place. He told me that he would be back in five to ten minutes and that he would arrive at the meeting, that he wouldn't be late. I came to the meeting of the municipal crisis staff in the municipal building, and I was asked whether I knew where the convoy was coming from carrying weapons and military equipment. I told them that I didn't know because I had spent the whole day at Kobiljaca touring the lines there and inspecting the positions and fortifications there. While we were discussing what this convoy was and where the convoy could come from and where it could pass through, we heard the noise of motor vehicles on the streets of Kiseljak, that is to say, there is just one main street, in fact. We heard noise there caused by vehicles, and we heard some shouting and voices outside. When I managed to go outside, I saw in front of the municipal building that there was a patrol vehicle of the Golf type, Volkswagen Golf, belonging to the civilian police, and that they had their rotation lights on, and a column with several heavy vehicles; and on the right-hand side, at some 20 or 15 metres from the municipal building, there were soldiers positioned belonging to the Territorial Defence and the Patriotic League together with Bakir, and they had their rifles cocked at the municipal building, ready to fire. I recognised some of the soldiers because they were from my own local community and I spent my childhood with some of them; we grew up together. I asked the members of MUP in the patrol vehicle, patrol car, what was happening. Where were they escorting the column to? It was at this point that one of the officers introduced himself -- I can't remember his name, but I know that he was a Bosniak Muslim, a member of the Foca police station -- and he was escorting the convoy with the intention of moving on towards Visoko. Of course, all the noise and the deployment of the soldiers led to reaction on the part of the HVO who were already positioned on the opposite side at a distance of some 30 metres away from the members of the Territorial Defence and the Patriotic League. An hour later, the convoy moved on, and when I asked Bakir why he failed to inform me about the arrival of the convoy and why he didn't tell me why he wanted to be taken to the crossroads in the first place, he said that he knew nothing about the convoy and that he just happened to be there by chance in the armed escort given to the convoy. That was how the incident concerning the convoy was closed. In the course of the morning, once again on the 4th of May, I was on my way back from the Kobiljaca feature and the positions there, Zvonko Anic was in the car with me and he, in fact, drove the car, and we were stopped at the Paleska Cuprija position at the entrance to the town of Kiseljak, we were stopped by Fabjan Dugandzic and his son Marko.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Are they Croats?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, they're Croats. Fabjan Dugandzic took out his pistol and cocked it at me and he had the gun at the ready, his son came up with an automatic rifle, and they cocked their weapons at me, they were half a metre away from me, and they were talking about what the HOS had done, the incident that occurred in their village, and they were protesting about that incident. They asked that incidents of this kind should not be repeated and said that he would liquidate me if they were. This particular incident which Fabjan and his son perpetrated was repeated two days later. This time, they turned their attention against the soldiers, members of the HVO and HOS, they directed their weapons against them, and on the 6th of May, 1992, they were engaged in engineering work on the 651 feature. This is a position at the front facing the Republika Srpska army. His justification and explanation for this was that if the Serbs were to notice a fortification going on, they would shell his house.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: That the Serbs would shell Dugandzics' house; is that right?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: He didn't allow fortification and trench-digging on his land for the defence of Kiseljak; is that true?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes. He came with his son, and he sent these recruits away, the recruits that were engaged in digging trenches.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Do you remember the 1st of May, 1992, trench-digging on that day and the conflict between the Croatian village of Palez and the Muslims?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. It was the village of Gornji Palez and the village of Duhri. There were joint village guards set up there that would patrol the village, a village watch, and they would be in the form of a patrol. They would move about the village patrolling the village. First of all, they took each other prisoner, but are neighbours, they are two neighbouring villages, the village of Gornji Palez and the village of Duhri, and when they had taken each other prisoner, later on this turned into general trench-digging and fortifications for military purposes, and they directed their -- that is, one village cocked its weapons at the other village, the Croatian village of Gornji Palez made fortifications towards the village of Duhri, and the village of Duhri, in turn, set up fortifications towards the village of Gornji Palez. This problem was solved on the 1st of May by the commander of the municipal staff of the HVO of Kiseljak, Tomislav Trutina, who himself was from the village of Gornji Palez, he was born there, it was his native village, and he held a meeting there with the representatives of both villages, and they decided that the trenches would be filled in and that the situation would be brought back to normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: My colleague has cautioned me that there might have been some problems over the translation. May I summarise and say that each of the two villages had dug trenches and turned against the other village; is that the sense?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: No, this happened on the 1st of May ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Once again, I have been told that it has been interpreted differently. So the trenches were dug and they faced the other village. So the village of Gornji Palez faced its trenches toward Duhri, Duhri dug their trenches and faced the other village; is that the sense of what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On the 1st of May, there was a conflict between the Muslims of Gromiljak with the civilian police force there. Did you take part in resolving that conflict?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I was on my way back sometime around 9.00 or 10.00 p.m., they were the afternoon hours, and they asked -- the members of the reserve force of the civilian police asked for my assistance because they were accused of not doing anything. People said they only spent their time in the police stations without actually doing much, and this created a certain amount of dissatisfaction both with the Bosniak Muslim people and with the Croatian people, especially with the military recruits who already at that time had been taking shifts, daily shifts, at the frontline towards the army of Republika Srpska. There was a conflict there too on the 1st of May. There was a round of gunfire in the evening, towards evening, by the armed Muslim Bosniak villagers towards the police station, the wartime police station positioned at Gromiljak. In talking to the members of that police station, they told me -- they told me what their names were, and on the basis of their names, I was able to conclude that they were Bosniak Muslims who, at the time, were performing their duty and were doing their shift. However, these conflicts with the reserve forces occurred in the Brestovsko local community as well, and in others too. I'll have a drink of water.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: The excess behaviours were attributed to the Vrazija Divizija, "Devil's Division," when they took over a certain amount of smuggled -- they smuggled cigarettes.

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, the members of a group that was called Vrazija Divizija, "Devil's Division," it wasn't, of course, a standard division made up of 8.000 to 12.000 soldiers, it was just an armed group numbering some 50 men, and in the middle of the day, it was perhaps noon or sometime in the early afternoon, they stormed the marketplace in Kiseljak and collected all the cigarette packages and cartons and all the valuable goods that were displayed there at a time when there were shortages of practically every commodity in Kiseljak. They paid nothing, of course, to the people selling those goods. After they had done this, they went on to the petrol pump, the only gas station that was open in Kiseljak at the time. They filled their vehicles up with petrol and went away without any intention of paying.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: How could we define, in the national sense, the Vrazija Divizija, "Devil's Division"? What ethnic group did they belong to? What about the tradesmen whose goods were stolen, what ethnic group did they belong to?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: I talked to some of the tradesmen because they complained themselves, they came to me to complain, and I talked to the attendants at the petrol pump, and they were Croats, and the members of the Devil's Division were mostly Croats, although there were some Bosniak Muslims within their ranks as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: On that particular day, there was a conflict between two HVO units around Cubren, was there not?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President, Your Honours. Cubren lies in this position here, it is the dominant feature in this entire Lepenica valley, that is the feature (indicating), and the former army had its radio relay links there and it used the feature within its communications and signals network. The border at the Cubren feature -- in fact, this feature was divided into two areas, so that the building where the staff was put up was on the territory of the Kiseljak municipality whereas the metal relay post with all the equipment was located, in fact, in the municipality of Kresevo. Although this tower was only ten or fifteen metres away from the building itself, it was a major problem for the two municipalities and the crisis staff of those two municipalities, that is to say, the civilian authorities of the Kresevo and Kiseljak municipalities, because they were not able to agree as to under whose competence and authority these facilities were. On that particular day, there was a confrontation, there was a confrontation with weapons and personnel between Kiseljak and Kresevo, the two municipalities.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So it was a Croat-Croat conflict. But on the 11th of May, part of Medvjednica sent in an ultimatum. Would you explain the circumstances of that ultimatum and who it was addressed to?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: This ultimatum was, in fact, just a continuation of a larger conflict or a larger friction which was going at the time which had to do with the lifting of the siege of Sarajevo. This ultimatum was sent to all the Croats living in the area of Medvjednica village to the effect that they should surrender their weapons and turn them over and the equipment, even though this village is at the frontline against the army of the Republika Srpska. The Territorial Defence consisted mostly of the Bosnian Muslims, and they sent this ultimatum to the Croats in the village of Medvjednica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: In which local commune is this village?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The village is partly in the Lepenica and partly in the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So this was on the 11th of May. As early as 12 May, the TO started shooting. Who were they shooting at?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The village of Sotnice is in the commune of Brestovsko, and in the course of the 11th of May, there was automatic rifle fire and the Croats were shot at. Croats were a minority in this village which was in the Kiseljak municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: You said that fire was opened against them. Now, who opened fire at them?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: The TO members, that is, the Bosniak Muslims. They lived in the majority there. Among them there may have been members of the Patriotic League, but there is a Muslim and Croat population there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: So the Croats in Fojnica and Busovaca looted a Muslim convoy on that day, on the 12th of May?

utterances.speaker: GENERAL TIHOMIR BLASKIC
utterances.text: Yes, this was a convoy, and it was the first time that the Territorial Defence was able to secure for itself some armoured vehicles. Up until then, such equipment was not around, at least we did not see them, and these were the first armoured vehicles which were later taken over by the Territorial Defence in Visoko. Your Honours, Mr. President, the Croats in Fojnica robbed this convoy and they took away almost all the equipment that this convoy was transporting, and later on they decided, together with the Busovaca HVO members, to take those vehicles, those armoured vehicles, along the road to Busovaca-Fojnica and then Kiseljak-Kresevo. While driving along this road, they shot around, and again it created a lot of excitement because they shot from heavy machine guns.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: Mr. President, we can stop at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: All right. We are going to stop for today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NOBILO
utterances.text: One more issue, Mr. President. If you will recall, Professor Jankovic, the artillery expert, the Trial Chamber ordered that the entire material about mortars be submitted, and here it is. We provide the entire --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: You want me to read it tonight, do you? All right. We can adjourn our session for today, and tomorrow we start at 10.00. All right. Court stands adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JORDA
utterances.text: 5.30 p.m., to be reconvened on Thursday, the 18th day of February, 1999, at 10.00 a.m.
